w:r.w:t: Welcome to Scrolls & Steel — a tabletop roleplaying game of ancient magic, dangerous roads, and characters defined not by the title they hold, but by the life they have lived. You will build a character who grows through practice, forges their own spells, inscribes their own enchantments, and carves their name into a world that does not give it out for free.

If you have played other tabletop roleplaying games, many concepts here will feel familiar: you and your friends sit around a table, you describe what your characters do, and dice determine whether the world cooperates. The differences run deeper, though, and they begin with a single idea — you are what you practice.

There are no rigid class progressions. Optional pre-built archetypes (Chapter 4) bundle skill selections together to get you started quickly, but the underlying system is entirely skill-based. A warrior who spends her evenings reading enchanting texts will, over time, become a warrior-enchanter. The game reflects the life you play, not the box you checked at character creation.

All checks use a d100 — two ten-sided dice. Roll equal to or under your effective skill to succeed. Higher skill means more room beneath it. Difficulty shifts your roll, not a pile of bonuses to track.
Spellcasters draw from a finite reserve of Magicka. No spell slots. You spend what you have, rest to recover it, and manage the gap between.
Spells and enchanted items are not selected from a fixed list — they are built from learned components. The spell list in Chapter 7 is a foundation, not a ceiling.
You track Health (how close to death you are) and Fatigue (how tired you are). Both matter in every fight. Running low on Fatigue makes you stumble; running out can kill you as surely as a blade.
When rules do not cover a situation, the Game Master makes a ruling and the game moves on. No rulebook can anticipate everything. When in doubt, call for a d100 roll against the most relevant skill.

Every character has eight core Attributes, each rated from 10 to 100. Attributes represent raw natural capacity — the ceiling of how good you can become in related skills, and the source of several derived statistics you will reference constantly during play.
Attributes do not add directly to your rolls. Instead, they cap what your skills can grow to, and feed into the derived numbers (Health, Magicka, Fatigue) that determine how long you survive.
Physical power. Governs melee damage with heavier weapons, carrying capacity, and feats of raw force.
Stamina and toughness. Governs Health points and your capacity to keep fighting after punishment.
Coordination and quickness. Governs turn order, damage with lighter weapons and ranged attacks, and dodge-based defense.
How fast you move. Governs movement in meters per turn.
Knowledge and analytical thought. Governs Magicka points and how readily you learn new spell effects.
Mental fortitude. Governs Magicka regeneration and resistance to mind-affecting magic.
Presence and charm. Governs social skill checks and the initial attitude of NPCs toward you.
Fortune. Either provides a flat bonus to every roll, or fuels a pool of Luck Dice — see the variant rule below.
Calculate these numbers at character creation.
Update them when the relevant Attribute changes.
During play, you only need to track three live numbers: current HP, current MP, and current FP.
END ÷ 5, round down. +2 per level after 1st.
INT ÷ 5, round down. +1 per level after 1st.
AGI ÷ 10, round down. Roll d10 at combat start and add this.
LCK ÷ 10, round down. Added to every skill roll (or replaced by Luck Dice — see variant).
STR ÷ 20, round down. Added to medium and heavy weapon damage.
AGI ÷ 20, round down. Added to light weapon and ranged damage.
SPD ÷ 2 (round to nearest 5) meters per turn. Minimum 10m.
Instead of a flat Luck Bonus added to every roll, some groups prefer fortune to be a dramatic, sparing resource.
LUCK POINTS POOL: Divide LCK by 30, rounding down. This is the number of Luck Points you receive
per long rest. LCK 30 = 1 point. LCK 60 = 2 points. LCK 90 = 3 points.
SPENDING A LUCK POINT: Declare before or after rolling. The roll automatically succeeds — no check
needed. You may not spend a Luck Point on a roll that has already been declared a critical failure
RECOVERY: Luck Points refill completely on a long rest. They do not refill on short rests.
This variant makes fortune feel genuinely miraculous — something saved for the moment that truly

Set all Attributes to 40, then distribute 30 extra points however you like. No Attribute may be below 10 or above 65 before racial bonuses; after racial bonuses, the cap is 75 at character creation. Through leveling and Feats, Attributes may be raised up to 100.

Skills are the most important numbers on your character sheet. There are 22 skills, each rated from 5 to 100. Your governing Attribute sets the ceiling — no skill may exceed the Attribute (or the average of two Attributes) that governs it, except through temporary magical enhancement.

Skills improve through use. The more you practice a skill in play, the more opportunities you get to advance it. This means a character's sheet slowly reshapes itself to match how they are actually played.
Maces, clubs, warhammers, and staves used as bludgeons.
Hand axes, war axes, and greataxes.
Polearms and thrusting weapons. Extended reach.
Active defense with a shield or two-handed weapon parry.
Defense and fluid movement without armor.
Running, swimming, climbing, and sustained movement.
Buying, selling, and negotiating to your advantage.
Brewing potions and poisons from raw ingredients.
Binding magical effects permanently into items.
Summoning creatures and binding spirits from other planes.
Bending physical laws — weight, water, locks, and more.
Offensive elemental magic: fire, frost, and shock.
Repairing and maintaining weapons and armor. Also used to craft basic equipment at a forge.
Attacks made while unarmed or with fist wraps and gauntlets.
Take the average (round down) as the cap. Long Blade on a character with STR 60 and AGI 40 has a cap of 50.

Your skill in an armor type actively improves its protection. As you become more experienced fighting in a particular armor, you learn how to move within it, angle it against blows, and maintain it for peak effectiveness.
A character wearing Chainmail (base AR 4) with Medium Armor skill 55 has an effective AR of 6 (4 base + 2 skill bonus).

At character creation, your 21 skills are divided into three tiers. This division is the single most important structural choice you make when building a character from scratch. Pre-built archetypes handle this for you.
The skills that define your character's core identity. Majors start at 40 and advance more quickly. Every 10 increases across your Major Skills triggers a Level Up.
Serious secondary pursuits. Minors start at 25 and advance at the same rate. Every 20 Minor Skill increases triggers a bonus Level Up.
Background exposure. Misc skills start at 5, require two meaningful uses per tick, and do not contribute to leveling up. They can still improve — it simply takes longer.
This optional rule rewards characters who focus on training the skills that match their core Attributes.
When you Level Up, calculate how many of each Attribute's governed skills improved since your last level:
You may still only choose 3 Attributes to increase per level up.

EXAMPLE: Oryn is a warrior with Long Blade (STR/AGI), Heavy Armor (END/STR), Block (STR/AGI), and Athletics (SPD/END) as Major skills — all trained hard this level. His STR governed skills improved 3 times (Long Blade, Block, Axe). He applies a ×3 multiplier to STR: rolls 3d4+3, getting 9+3 = 12. STR 55 becomes 67. Meanwhile his INT governed 0 skills — he rolls 1d4+1 for it if chosen, getting a modest 3. This rewards playing your archetype and makes divergence from your build feel mechanically meaningful.

Archetypes are fully assembled character packages designed to get you to the table in minutes. Each includes a spread of Attributes, chosen Major and Minor skills, and an archetype-specific bonus. They are organized into three broad categories — Martial, Stealth & Social, and Arcane — so you can quickly find a role that suits you.

If you are using an archetype, skip Steps 2 and 3 of character creation (Chapter 11). Your Attributes and skill tiers are already handled. You still choose your Race and Birthsign, calculate derived statistics, and select starting equipment.
Nothing prevents a Knight from picking up Alchemy, or a Nightblade from wearing plate. Archetypes set where you begin, not where you end.

Warriors, soldiers, and those for whom the answer to most problems is a weapon held in the right hand. Martial archetypes differ primarily in how they hit, how long they last, and how many things they can hit at once.

When a Knight enters a room, the room gets smaller. Greatswords, war axes, two-handed hammers — these are their instruments, and the damage they deal is extraordinary. Every swing burns Fatigue, so Knights are at their best in short, decisive engagements: kick in the door, clear the room, find somewhere to breathe. They falter in extended attrition fights and they are not subtle — but when they are at full Fatigue with a greatsword in both hands, there is almost nothing that hits harder.
Primary damage dealer. Ends fights before the rest of the group runs low on resources. Veteran Knights learn to pace themselves and trust their allies to cover their flanks.
STR 65 END 55 AGI 35 SPD 35 INT 25 WIL 25 PER 35 LCK 30
Blunt Weapon, Axe, Long Blade, Heavy Armor, Athletics
Block, Medium Armor, Speechcraft, Acrobatics, Vitalism
+5 to STR damage bonus calculations. Start with an Iron Greatsword and Iron Chainmail.

The Shield-Brother is the wall that holds. One weapon, one shield, and absolute refusal to go down — this archetype is built around surviving punishment that would collapse anyone else. Their Block skill makes incoming damage unreliable for enemies; their Vitalism dabbling lets them patch themselves mid-fight. Less raw damage than the Knight, but vastly more durable. In a long dungeon, that trade-off often wins.

The party's anchor. When things go wrong — and they will — the Shield-Brother holds ground while allies recover. They are also typically the one who talks to the city guard, because they look like they have survived worse.
STR 55 END 60 AGI 45 SPD 35 INT 25 WIL 30 PER 30 LCK 25
Long Blade, Block, Heavy Armor, Athletics, Vitalism
Blunt Weapon, Medium Armor, Speechcraft, Acrobatics, Short Blade
+1 AR when using a shield. Start with an Iron Longsword, Iron Shield, and Iron Chainmail.

Fast, precise, and dangerous at close range — the Duelist's power comes from speed rather than raw strength. Two weapons mean two attacks per round, trading the penalty for relentless pressure that few opponents can weather. Agility drives both skill checks and damage, and their movement options make them difficult to pin down. Their weakness is durability: light armor and no shield means every hit that lands hurts.
Damage dealer with mobility. Thrives when choosing engagements; struggles when the enemy controls the space. Experienced Duelists communicate: 'Keep their attention, and I will bleed them out.'
STR 40 END 40 AGI 65 SPD 50 INT 25 WIL 25 PER 35 LCK 30
Short Blade, Long Blade, Acrobatics, Light Armor, Athletics
Second attack has no penalty, and feats that would reduce the penalty make your second attack easier. Start with two Iron Shortswords and Leather Armor.
Distance, Patience, and a Steady Hand

Damage dealt from beyond reach is damage you never have to absorb. Rangers keep enemies at range with bows and crossbows, ending threats before they become problems. Their Sneak and Athletics make them exceptional scouts — they often know what is in a room before their party reaches the door. If cornered in melee, they manage with a short blade, but staying out of arm's reach is always the plan.
The party's eyes and first source of damage. They call positions, fire from cover, and move through terrain that slows everyone else.
STR 35 END 45 AGI 65 SPD 45 INT 30 WIL 25 PER 25 LCK 35
Marksman, Sneak, Light Armor, Athletics, Short Blade
Acrobatics, Long Blade, Alchemy, Block, Vitalism
Can fire a bow twice per turn a set number of times each combat equal to their character level. Start with a Short Bow, 20 arrows, and Leather Armor.

The Crusader fights in heavy plate and carries both a weapon and a working knowledge of Vitalism magic. They are not as offensively powerful as a pure Knight, nor as magically capable as a dedicated Priest — but they can do both, in the same encounter, without stopping. Healing themselves mid-combat, resisting disease and poison, and outlasting opponents are the Crusader's defining gifts.
The party member who never quite dies. Excellent at protecting allies by drawing fire, buying time, and keeping everyone functional when things go badly wrong.
STR 55 END 55 AGI 35 SPD 30 INT 30 WIL 55 PER 35 LCK 25
Long Blade, Heavy Armor, Vitalism, Block, Athletics
Blunt Weapon, Medium Armor, Speechcraft, Divination, Conjuration
Vitalism spells while in heavy armor cost 1 less MP (min 1). Start with an Iron Longsword, Iron Shield, Iron Chainmail, and two Apprentice Vitalism spells.

Not every problem requires a sword. These archetypes excel at getting places they should not be, learning things they should not know, and talking their way out of situations they probably should not have gotten into.

A scout wreathed in illusions moves through an occupied fortress, marking patrol routes in her mind. An assassin steps out of invisibility behind a mage, drives a dagger in, and vanishes before the body hits the floor. The Nightblade merges arcane capability with lethal precision — they use Illusion magic to get into position, then make the most of it.
Shines where preparation meets opportunity. Requires more planning than a Knight, but a well-positioned Nightblade can eliminate a target before the rest of the party draws steel.
STR 30 END 35 AGI 60 SPD 40 INT 50 WIL 40 PER 35 LCK 25
Short Blade, Sneak, Illusion, Acrobatics, Light Armor
Long Blade, Divination, Alteration, Athletics, Security
+1d6 damage from undetected position (once per combat unless re-hidden). Start with an Iron Dagger, Leather Armor, and two Apprentice Illusion spells.
Locks, Pockets, and Getting Away With It

A pickpocket relieves a wealthy merchant of his purse before the crowd's applause for a street performer fades. A burglar scales a garden wall and vanishes into a manor. A con artist gets a city official to sign something he did not mean to. Rogues master the non-combat space — they open doors that should not open, acquire things not for sale, and gather information meant to stay buried.

Invaluable where raw force is wrong. Security and Speechcraft together mean most obstacles can be circumvented rather than confronted. In combat, a well-placed opening strike from hiding can change a fight's calculus entirely.
STR 30 END 35 AGI 60 SPD 50 INT 40 WIL 25 PER 55 LCK 40
Short Blade, Sneak, Security, Acrobatics, Speechcraft
Light Armor, Marksman, Mercantile, Athletics, Illusion
Re-roll one failed Speechcraft or Security roll per short rest. Start with a Lockpick Set, Iron Dagger, Leather Armor, and 100 gold.

A traveling performer finishes a ballad in a crowded tavern, then quietly extracts three secrets, a business proposition, and a map from the people who bought her drinks. A court herald speaks exactly the right words to defuse a situation thirty seconds from bloodshed. Bards are the game's ultimate social characters — they move through every level of society with ease, turning conversation into leverage and performance into access.
Most valuable in campaigns with significant social and political content. Their broad knowledge makes them the party's best source of 'wait, I know something about this.'
STR 25 END 35 AGI 40 SPD 40 INT 45 WIL 35 PER 70 LCK 40
Speechcraft, Illusion, Mercantile, Short Blade, Acrobatics
Vitalism, Alchemy, Light Armor, Athletics, Sneak
May substitute Speechcraft for any PER-adjacent skill roll once per short rest. Start with a Simple Instrument, Iron Dagger, Traveler's Clothes, and two Apprentice Illusion spells.
Information Is the Only Currency That Matters

Every faction wants something, and the Spy makes it their business to know what. They work at the intersection of illusory magic and high-society Speechcraft — not skulking through shadows like a thief, but moving openly through the world with a different face and a perfected backstory. They are the archetype for players who want the game to reward careful preparation, patience, and the slow accumulation of exactly the right leverage.

At their best when the party needs to infiltrate something rather than attack it. Their magic keeps them protected; their social skills keep them functional once inside. Requires a GM willing to run complex social environments with real stakes.
STR 25 END 30 AGI 45 SPD 35 INT 55 WIL 40 PER 65 LCK 35
Illusion, Speechcraft, Sneak, Mercantile, Short Blade
Alteration, Divination, Security, Acrobatics, Light Armor

Once per short rest, create a convincing false identity — Speechcraft rolls to maintain it are Easy (−10). Start with a Disguise Kit, Iron Dagger, one set of decent clothing, two Apprentice Illusion spells, 100 gold.
Everything Has a Price. Knowing It Is the Skill.

The Fence is not primarily a thief, an assassin, or a con artist — they are a broker. They know who buys unusual things and who wants unusual things done. Their Mercantile skill is exceptional, their Speechcraft is precise, and their Security skill exists because the line between knowing where treasure is and acquiring it is thinner than most people acknowledge.

Shines in campaigns where the party needs money, information, or introductions they cannot get by asking nicely. A skilled Fence can transform random dungeon finds into faction connections and maps nobody else has.
STR 30 END 35 AGI 45 SPD 35 INT 55 WIL 30 PER 65 LCK 50
Mercantile, Speechcraft, Security, Sneak, Short Blade
Light Armor, Acrobatics, Alchemy, Illusion, Athletics

Always knows the approximate value of any item on sight. Appraise items' value without a roll. Sell prices treated as if Mercantile were 20 higher. Can sell stolen items to any merchant that would normally accept them. Start with Iron Dagger, Merchant Kit, 150 gold, and one named contact (work with DM).

Arcane archetypes trade physical resilience and martial capability for access to the most powerful and versatile tools in the game. What they share is reliance on Magicka and the need for careful resource management.

A soldier in chainmail channels lightning through her sword as she closes on a formation. A combat veteran wades into melee, using magic as a force multiplier rather than a primary offense. The Battle-Mage refuses the mage's traditional fragility — they wear real armor, carry a real weapon, and managing both Magicka and Fatigue simultaneously is the central challenge and satisfaction of this archetype.

A self-sufficient frontliner who brings options pure warriors lack. Opens with spellfire, presses with steel, finishes with whatever is necessary. Slower to master than either pure warriors or pure mages, but extraordinarily difficult to counter.
STR 45 END 45 AGI 35 SPD 30 INT 55 WIL 45 PER 25 LCK 30
Elementalism, Long Blade, Medium Armor, Alteration, Block
Vitalism, Conjuration, Athletics, Heavy Armor, Divination
+1 MP recovered on short rest. Start with an Iron Longsword, Iron Chainmail, and three Apprentice Elementalism spells.

An Adept Fireball turns a bandit ambush into a memory. A chain of lightning jumps from mercenary to mercenary. At full Magicka, the Sorcerer is the most offensively powerful character in any encounter. The cost is everything else: no armor, marginal melee ability, and an MP pool that empties fast at higher ranks. Good positioning is not an option — it is a survival requirement.
Glass cannon in the most direct sense. When protected, they end fights. When exposed, they collapse. Playing one well means constant communication with your party.
STR 20 END 25 AGI 30 SPD 30 INT 75 WIL 65 PER 30 LCK 30
Illusion, Vitalism, Enchanting, Unarmored, Short Blade
+2 bonus MP. Elementalism spells cost 1 less MP (min 1). Start with an Ironwood Staff and three Apprentice spells.

A battlefield healer moves between the wounded, never stopping. A temple scholar lays hands on the fevered and watches sickness retreat. The Priest keeps people alive — not glamorously, not violently, but reliably. Their Conjuration lets them call allies when direct action is unavoidable, and their Alchemy supplements healing with prepared potions and curative draughts.

A Priest's contribution is measured in the distance between 'party survives this dungeon' and 'party does not.' Priests anchor many campaigns' moral tensions — questions about life, death, and obligation land hardest on the one who can heal.
STR 20 END 40 AGI 30 SPD 30 INT 55 WIL 70 PER 45 LCK 30
Alteration, Illusion, Light Armor, Enchanting, Athletics
Vitalism spells cost 1 less MP (min 1). Potions brewed by you that restore HP, MP, or FP also restore +2 HP. Start with an Ironwood Staff and three Apprentice Vitalism spells.

A mage at the back of a room gestures, and something answers from beyond the veil. A bound blade materializes in an outstretched hand. A creature of smoke and fury stands between its summoner and an axe. Summoners fight through proxies — called entities and bound weapons that take damage the summoner does not. At full resources they can double a party's effective combat presence. Without Magicka, they are nearly helpless.
Rewards patience and preparation. Not a front-line combatant; a force multiplier who keeps the actual combatants alive by providing things for enemies to fight instead.
STR 20 END 30 AGI 30 SPD 30 INT 70 WIL 65 PER 30 LCK 30
May maintain one extra summon at a time. Summons last +1 minute. Start with four Apprentice/Journeyman Conjuration spells.

An entire patrol of guards passes within three feet of a motionless party, none of them seeing a thing. A fearsome beast turns on its handler, driven to frenzy by a whispered working. Illusionists win by preventing the fight from occurring at all, or by so thoroughly disrupting an enemy's ability to function that the fight is over before it starts.
The most unconventional arcane archetype — and the one with the broadest applicability outside combat. They rarely deal damage. They often decide outcomes.
STR 20 END 30 AGI 40 SPD 35 INT 65 WIL 55 PER 60 LCK 30
Short Blade, Acrobatics, Vitalism, Enchanting, Mercantile
Illusion spells cost 1 less MP (min 1). Use Illusion in place of Sneak once per combat. Start with three Apprentice Illusion spells.

Two dozen vials, carefully labeled, fill a satchel. Each was brewed over the last three days and will accomplish something a sword simply cannot. A poison slips into a target's wine. A paralyzing splash stops a charging warrior. A curative draught keeps an ally functional for three more rounds. The Witch does not win fights in real time — she wins them before they start.

A hybrid utility character with enormous depth. Thrown potions and poisons give real offensive capability that bypasses armor. Magic schools fill the gaps. Witches tend to be underestimated until someone is suddenly paralyzed.
STR 25 END 40 AGI 35 SPD 30 INT 65 WIL 60 PER 30 LCK 40
Brew one extra potion per long rest. Thrown alchemicals gain +1 magnitude. Start with an Alchemical Kit, Mortar & Pestle, Iron Dagger, and two Apprentice spells.

A traveling apothecary moves through markets buying mundane herbs that everyone else overlooks, knowing exactly what combinations they conceal. An experimental brewmaster lobs a shattering vial into a crowd of enemies. A merchant-philosopher who has never met a situation where a correctly applied substance could not improve it.

Their greatest asset is preparation and self-sufficiency. Identifies every ingredient encountered, always knows what the party needs before a dungeon, fills gaps with bottled solutions. Thrown potions make them a real offensive threat when needed.
STR 30 END 40 AGI 40 SPD 35 INT 70 WIL 45 PER 40 LCK 55
Alchemy, Mercantile, Short Blade, Athletics, Vitalism
Security, Speechcraft, Light Armor, Enchanting, Divination
+1 property revealed when tasting an unknown ingredient. May identify any potion without a roll. Start with a basic Alchemical Kit (mortar & pestle), Iron Dagger, and 100 gold.
Every Item Is a Spell Waiting to Be Written

Piece by piece, a party equipped by a skilled Enchanter becomes more than the sum of its parts. A shortsword that bites with frost. Boots that muffle every step. A ring that makes its wearer slightly harder to look at directly. Enchanters do not change fights through what they do in combat — they change fights through what they have done for the last week.
The party's artificer and force multiplier. Modest in short-term contribution. By mid-campaign, every party member carries two or three items they made, and the gap is substantial.
STR 25 END 35 AGI 35 SPD 30 INT 70 WIL 65 PER 30 LCK 40
Vitalism, Elementalism, Speechcraft, Security, Short Blade
When making constant-effect enchantments, ignore the magnitude penalty. Start with an Enchanting Toolkit, one filled Lesser Soul Gem, and 50 gold.

Every character in Scrolls & Steel was born under one of the thirteen constellations recognized by Aethermoor's astronomers and mystics. Birthsigns are chosen at character creation and provide a permanent boon that tilts a character toward a particular style of play.

Birthsigns are roughly equal in power — they are not ranks, and no sign is objectively better than another. Each leans toward a different approach: raw power, utility, resilience, magic, or fortune. Choose the sign that best represents who your character is, or roll 1d13 if you prefer to let fate decide.
Birthsigns are permanent. They cannot be changed after character creation. A few signs grant limited-use abilities — these refresh on a long rest unless otherwise noted.

The Ironstar rises in late autumn, a compact cluster that ancient sailors called the Shield-Fist. Those born under it are said to have iron in their blood and conflict in their nature — not cruelty, but an attunement to struggle.
Once per combat, when you are hit by an attack that would deal more than half your current HP in damage, reduce that damage by 1d10 (rolled after the hit is determined).
+5 to Block and Heavy Armor skills at character creation.
The Wandering Eye — Born Under Uncertainty

A lone star that drifts visibly against the fixed firmament across a lifetime — an optical illusion, astronomers now say, though mystics disagree. Those born under it are restless, perceptive, and rarely where you expect them to be.

Your Luck Bonus (or Luck Dice pool) increases by 1. Additionally, once per long rest, you may re-roll any single d100 roll and keep whichever result you prefer. However, your restless nature makes sustained focus difficult: you have a −5 penalty to all Concentration-type checks (holding spells, maintaining grips, resisting distractions).
+5 to Sneak and Mercantile at character creation.
The Scholar's Lantern — Born Under Knowledge

A dim, steady constellation that burns throughout the year. Scholars claim it never sets — it simply becomes invisible against the dawn. Those born under it learn faster, reason more clearly, and remember things they were never taught.
+10 to Intelligence at character creation (max 75 after racial bonuses). Additionally, when you successfully advance a Miscellaneous skill, you may advance it by 1d6 instead of 1d4.
+5 to any two magic school skills of your choice.

A sprawling constellation in the shape of a thorned branch, visible only in deep winter. Those born under it are difficult to kill — not through any visible toughness, but through a stubborn persistence that outlasts situations that should have finished them.
+10 to Endurance at character creation (max 75). Your death threshold increases by 2 (you die at a lower negative HP total).
Once per long rest, when you would be Knocked Down, you may choose to only become Staggered instead.
The Silver Tongue — Born Under Eloquence
A crescent-shaped constellation associated in folklore with honeybees, silver coins, and broken promises. Those born under it find words come easily — almost suspiciously so.
+10 to Personality at character creation (max 75). NPCs' starting Disposition toward you is +5 higher than it would otherwise be.
+10 to Speechcraft and +5 to Mercantile at character creation.
The Ashen Crown — Born Under Loss

A constellation that appears only after major catastrophes, according to myth — though it rises every year regardless of what happens below. Those born under it are marked by something — a resilience born from having already survived something terrible, or perhaps the expectation that they will.
When stabilizing an ally, they gain HP equal to 1d6 + your Vitalism or END modifier, whichever is higher.
+10 to Vitalism and +5 to END at character creation.
The Pale Archer — Born Under Precision
A long, thin constellation oriented like a drawn bow. Those born under it have an unnerving capacity for patience — they wait, they watch, and when they act, they rarely miss.
Your critical success threshold improves by 1 (critical hits occur on rolls of 1–3 instead of 1–2, before skill adjustments). Additionally, ranged attacks ignore the first 2 points of a target's AR.

A bright, comfortable constellation associated with hospitality, cooking fires, and the warmth of company. Those born under it recover faster, sustain more effort, and tend to bring out the best in those around them.
Recover +2 FP per minute of rest instead of 1d4. Additionally, once per short rest, you can spend a bonus action to give an ally within short range (10m) who can hear you 1d6 FP.

A star pattern that is defined by what is not there — a rough ring of dim stars around a patch of empty sky. Mystics argue about what it represents. Those born under it are comfortable in the dark, in empty places, and with things that have no name.
+10 to Willpower at character creation (max 75). Spell absorption effects are 10% more effective. Once per long rest, cast any Apprentice spell you know at no MP cost.
The Crimson Hart — Born Under Passion
A red-tinged constellation shaped, to some eyes, like a leaping deer. Those born under it burn with something — conviction, fury, love, obsession. It does not matter which.
Once per combat, you may declare a Burning Strike before rolling an attack. If the attack hits, double the damage before applying AR. If it misses, you lose 2 FP from the overextension.
+10 to STR or AGI (choose) at character creation.
The Steadfast Wheel — Born Under Prosperity

A circular constellation associated with mills, turning seasons, and the movement of goods. Those born under it understand value — what things cost, what they are worth, and what the difference between those two numbers can buy.

Your Mercantile sell prices are 10% better than the table indicates at all skill levels. Additionally, once per long rest, you may appraise an item and learn its exact value and any enchantments it carries (no Enchanting roll needed).

A dense, intricate constellation that rewards patient observation — the more you look, the more patterns emerge. Those born under it are makers: they understand structure, they build things that last, and they leave marks on the world.
Enchanting and Alchemy rolls are made at Advantage. Additionally, items you enchant or craft are 1 tier higher.
+10 to Enchanting or Alchemy (choose) and +5 to the other.
The Empty Throne — Born Under Command

A large, prominent constellation shaped like a high-backed chair with no one in it. Those born under it are noticed. They are listened to. Whether that is a gift or a burden depends entirely on what they say.

Followers, hirelings, summoned entities, and allied party members within Short range (10m) of you apply -5 to all skill rolls. When you use a Speechcraft-adjacent ability with a once-per-short-rest limit, you may use it one additional time per short rest.

Characters in Scrolls & Steel grow through doing. A warrior who practices her blade every fight will, given enough fights, be a better sword fighter. A mage who pushes the limits of his Elementalism school will eventually stop flinching at Expert-rank spells. There is no experience point tally and no separate leveling currency — the process of play is the advancement system.

After any encounter, scene, or challenge in which you made a meaningful use of a skill — success or failure — place a small tick mark (✓) next to that skill. 'Meaningful' means the roll mattered: not a trivial action, but not necessarily a dramatic success either. The guard you failed to sneak past counts. The guard who never saw you also counts. But stealth-rolling down an empty corridor does not.
What you track is exposure to challenge. Growth comes from being tested, not from succeeding. Each skill may only accumulate one tick between long rests.
Roll d100. If the result is higher than your current skill rating, the skill increases by 1d4. Write the new total.
If the result is equal to or lower than your rating, no improvement — you need harder tests to keep growing.
Erase the tick mark regardless of outcome.
A Miscellaneous skill requires TWO meaningful uses to earn a single tick. Same advancement procedure applies.

ONE TICK PER SKILL PER REST: A skill may only accumulate one tick between long rests, regardless of how many times it is used meaningfully. Additional meaningful uses after the first do not add more ticks — the skill has already been sufficiently tested and the body needs rest to absorb the growth. This encourages breadth of activity over grinding a single skill.
Vera has Sneak 47. She sneaks past two guards successfully and fails on a third. She marks a tick.
On long rest she rolls d100 and gets 61 — higher than 47. She rolls 1d4 and gets 3. Sneak becomes 50.
Three months later, Sneak is 78. She rolls 55 — lower than 78. The challenges she faced were no longer

A Level Up represents a significant milestone of personal growth — not just improved skills, but a fundamental sharpening of instinct, awareness, and capacity. You don't tick off experience points to reach it; you improve specific skills until the sum of that improvement crosses a threshold.

You track two separate Growth Tallies on your sheet: one for Major Skills and one for Minor Skills. Each time a Major Skill increases by any amount, mark it in the Major Tally. When the Major Tally reaches 10, you gain a Level. Every time the Minor Tally reaches 20, you gain a bonus Level. Both tallies reset to 0 after triggering.
Choose 3 Attributes to increase. Each increases by 1d4+1 (minimum 2). See the Practiced Growth variant rule in Chapter 3 for multiplier-based gains.
Maximum HP increases by +2, maximum FP increases by +1, and maximum MP increases by +1. This goes on top of your ‘base’ maximums provided by your attribute scores (see chapter 2)
You gain one Feat (see below). You may bank it and spend it later when you meet a prerequisite.
Every 5 levels, you gain a Boon (see the Boons section).
Attributes may be raised to a maximum of 100 through advancement. No Attribute may exceed 75 at character creation (after racial bonuses).
No skill may exceed its governing Attribute ceiling.
Enchantments, potions, and certain abilities can push past these caps temporarily.

Feats are specialized techniques and trained mastery that represent a deeper layer of a character's development — things that cannot be acquired simply by grinding a skill, but emerge from a particular combination of experience and deliberate focus. You gain one Feat at character creation and one more at each Level Up. You may bank Feats and spend them when you are ready.
Each Feat has a Prerequisite — a minimum skill or Attribute rating required before it can be taken.
Gaining one Feat per level is the default rule. Groups should treat this as a starting point:
• Every level (default): Characters feel frequently rewarded and grow quickly.
• Every 2 levels: Feat choices feel more weighty; works well for longer campaigns.
• Every 3–4 levels: Feats are rare and significant; appropriate for gritty, slow-burn settings.
There is no objectively correct frequency. Adjust based on how fast your group levels and how much
After a successful Long Blade hit, make one additional attack at +20 to roll. Once per combat.
On a successful Block, your next attack against that attacker is made with advantage.
Critical blunt hits (natural 1–2) automatically Stagger the target.
No longer suffer the +10 roll penalty when you move and attack in the same round.
Lose 1 less FP per round in combat (minimum 1).
Your Axe attacks bypass 1 point of the target's AR.
If you move away from a target and then attack with a spear, deal +1d6 bonus damage.
No FP cost for ranged attacks. Ranged critical hits occur on a natural roll of 1–4.
When you hit 0 FP, you have one additional round before Staggered applies.
Off-hand attack penalty reduced from +20 to +10 to roll.
When wielding a one-handed weapon with a shield, you no longer suffer the +5 attack roll penalty.
Once per long rest, before making an attack, declare it Armor-Piercing. That hit ignores the target's AR entirely.
Once per long rest, make one attack that completely ignores AR. (This is a second use, separate from Armor Piercer.)
Your weapon attacks always deal a minimum of 1 damage on a hit, even if AR would reduce it to 0.
Once per combat, when an attack is declared against you, make an AGI check (d100 vs AGI). On success, the attack misses entirely, regardless of the attacker's roll.

Your understanding of the spiritual world lets your strikes reach where steel alone cannot. Your non-silver, non-magical weapons can damage incorporeal entities (ghosts, wraiths, shades) at half damage. Silver and magical weapons still deal full damage.

Choose one specific creature type (e.g., skeletons, goblins, wolves, trolls). Against that type, you gain: - 10 to attack rolls, +1 damage per hit, and advantage on checks to track, identify, or recall information about them. You may take this feat multiple times, choosing a new creature type each time.

Choose one specific weapon (e.g., Steel Longsword, Iron War Axe). When wielding that exact weapon, you gain +5 to attack rolls, +1 damage, and your critical success threshold improves by 1 (crits occur on rolls under Skill / 9 instead of / 10). If your favored weapon is lost or destroyed, you may designate a new one after one week of practice, but it must be of a weapon skill that is above 50.

Before making an attack, you may declare an Armor Breach attempt. Make a Hard roll (your weapon skill at +20). On a success, the target's AR is reduced by 2 for the rest of combat. On a failure, your attack misses automatically and you lose 1 FP from the awkward swing. You may attempt this any number of times per combat, but each failed attempt after the first adds a cumulative +5 to all your attack rolls for the rest of the combat.

Your Reaction strikes against disengaging enemies do not suffer the normal +10 difficulty penalty — they are made at Normal difficulty. Additionally, when you successfully hit an enemy with a Reaction strike, that enemy’s movement ends immediately — they cannot complete their disengage. Once per combat.

When you attack the same enemy twice in a row (your previous attack this combat was against this target), gain +5 to the attack roll. Each consecutive hit against the same target increases this bonus by 1 (to a maximum of +15). The bonus resets if you attack a different target or miss.

Once per combat, when you hit an enemy with a melee weapon, you may declare a Sweeping Strike. Make a secondary attack roll at +20 against a different enemy adjacent to the first target. On a hit, deal half your weapon’s damage (rounded down). Stagger effects and crits do not apply to the secondary target.

When you move and attack in the same turn, you no longer suffer the +10 attack roll penalty. Additionally, if you attack a different target than your previous attack this round, gain -5 to the second attack roll. Designed for fluid, mobile fighters who never stay still.

When grappling, you gain Advantage on your Athletics rolls to initiate and maintain holds. Creatures you have grappled cannot break free on their first attempt — they must spend two consecutive Actions before their opposed roll is allowed. Additionally, you may make one Fistfighting Strike against a creature you are actively grappling as a bonus action each round.
Regain 1 FP at the start of each of your turns. At Athletics 80 and AGI 80, this becomes 2 FP, and at 100 for both, this becomes 3 FP.
+1 AR in Light Armor. +10m movement while wearing only Light Armor.
+1 AR in Medium Armor. Never penalized to Initiative from Medium Armor.
+1 AR in Heavy Armor. Halve FP penalties from Heavy Armor.
While unarmored, attempt to vanish at the end of any round you did not attack and are out of direct line of sight.
Block without a shield using your weapon as a parry, at +10 to the roll.

Once per combat, when you declare a Block before an attack and the attacker’s roll would have missed anyway (their roll exceeded their effective skill without your Block), your Block Reaction is not consumed. You reset your guard smoothly and may Block again this round.

You treat all enemies within 5m as Engaged for purposes of Reaction strikes when they attempt to move. You may make Reaction strikes against any creature in this radius that moves without Disengaging, not just those who attacked you directly. This ability is active as long as you have your Reaction available.

Once per combat, when an adjacent ally is hit by an attack, you may choose to take that hit instead. You must be aware of the attack and adjacent to the ally. You cannot use Block against a hit you chose to intercept this way.

Once per combat, when you declare a Block and the attacker’s roll would have missed anyway (their roll exceeded their effective skill regardless of your Block), you recover your Block Reaction — it is not used. This represents recognizing the blow was going wide and resetting your guard smoothly.

When an attack is made against you, spend a Reaction (once per round) to roll your Block skill. On success, the attack deflects entirely — dealing no damage. This is separate from the standard Block reaction.

Your weapon attacks reduce the target's effective AR by 2 for the purpose of calculating damage. This is a property of your attack — not a permanent debuff. Stacks with Armor Piercer but cannot reduce AR below 0.

Your critical success threshold improves by 1. This feat can be taken multiple times — each time it is taken, the threshold expands by an additional 1. Requires increasing that skill by at least 5 before taking this feat again.
Immediately increase two Attributes of your choice by 5 each, or one Attribute by 10. Can be taken multiple times.
Increase your max HP by 2 x your current level. You gain +2 additional HP per level up (stacks: +2 per time this feat is taken).
Increase your max FP by 2 x your current level. You gain +2 additional FP per level up (stacks: +2 per time this feat is taken).
Increase your max MP by an amount equal to your current level. You gain +1 additional MP per level up (stacks: +1 per time this feat is taken).

Choose one skill when you take this feat. Between long rests, that skill may accumulate up to 2 ticks instead of 1. If both ticks are earned, roll advancement twice at rest and take the better result. This represents focused obsessive practice with a specific discipline. You may take this feat multiple times, applying it to a different skill each time.

You cannot be knocked Prone by physical attacks, shoves, or non-magical forced movement. You may still be knocked Prone by magic or terrain. If you would be Knocked Down from Staggered + damage, you are instead only Staggered.

You may throw potions and poisons up to Long range (30m) instead of the standard Short range (10m). At Very Long range (60m) the throw is made at +10 to the Marksman roll. The thrown item still has a 2m radius area of effect on impact.
Choose one school. Spells from that school cost 1 less MP (min 1). Can stack, choosing additional magic schools each time.
Any school 50 + Long or Short Blade 40

Designate a weapon or staff as an arcane focus for one school of magic. After making an attack with that weapon, you can immediately cast another spell from that school that you know with a +2 MP cost. Can change to a different weapon during a long rest, but you can only have one at a time.
Once per long rest, cast one Journeyman spell at no MP cost.
Recover +2 additional MP on short rests.
Critical casting threshold improves: crits occur on rolls under School Skill ÷ 8 instead of ÷ 10.
Once per long rest, cast the same spell twice simultaneously, and you are able to choose new targets for this. Pay full MP for both.
Once per combat, spend 2 MP as a reaction to reduce incoming magic damage by 1d6.
Detect the presence of souls within 5m passively. No roll or MP required.
Vitalism spells cast on others heal +1d4 additional HP.
Once per long rest, when you fail a spell cast (not a critical failure), you may treat it as a success instead. At skill 95 in that school, this ability gains a second use per long rest.

Once per round, you may sacrifice HP to restore MP. Roll 1d6: lose that many HP and regain half that amount (round down) as MP. You may use this even if it would reduce you to 0 HP, but doing so immediately causes you to fall Unconscious.
Once per round, you may roll 1d6: you lose that many HP and regain that many MP. You cannot use this ability if you are at 1 HP.

When you cast an Elementalism spell, you may bind a second damage type to it. The spell's total damage is split: the secondary type deals half (round down) and the primary type deals the rest. For example, a spell dealing 10 fire damage can instead deal 5 fire and 5 frost. The total damage does not increase. You choose the secondary element each time you cast.

When a summoned entity you control is reduced to 0 HP for any reason, you may immediately spend MP equal to half its original casting cost (round up) to restore it to full HP. The entity does not disappear and takes no action on that turn. You may use this once per summon per combat.

Once per short rest, you may create a brief sensory distraction within 15m: a sound, a flicker of movement, or a visual shadow. Enemies who might react must make a WIL roll (+0) or spend their next move investigating. Additionally, Illusion spells you cast last one additional round before requiring concentration.

Once per long rest, spend 10 minutes in quiet meditation to recover MP equal to your WIL ÷ 10 (round down, minimum 1). This recovery occurs outside of normal short rest MP recovery and does not count as a short rest for recovering other attributes.

You form a mental link with summoned entities under your control. You may give them simple tactical instructions (attack this target, guard that ally, hold this position) as a free action on your turn. Without this feat, summoned entities default to attacking the nearest enemy each round and cannot follow complex commands.

When an enemy caster summons an entity within Long range (30m) of you, you may spend your Reaction and an amount of MP equal to the summon’s casting cost to immediately banish it as it arrives. The summon is removed before it acts. The enemy’s MP is still spent. You must be aware of the summoning (you can see or hear it). Once per combat.
Can be taken multiple times. When crafting a spell of this school, reduce the MP cost by 1. At skill level 100, this discount becomes 2.
You gain the ability to concentrate on 2 spells at once. While concentrating on 2 spells, WIL checks to maintain them are made with a -20 penalty to the roll, and if broken, both spells end.
Once per round, if attacking undetected, you have advantage on your attack roll.
Once per short rest, you can re-roll one Speechcraft check. Accept the second result.
Never critically fail on Security checks.
You are able to spend 10 minutes inspecting an item to determine its approximate market value, not including enchantments. Sell prices are 10% better.
Poisons you brew deal +1 damage and last one additional round.
Illusion and charm effects targeting you require two successful rolls, not one.
Thrown potions gain +1 magnitude. Prime and throw as a single action.
Poisons on a weapon last 2 hits (3 hits with Alchemy 80+).

You may use your Security skill to actively detect traps. When moving through an area you suspect contains traps, declare a Search action and roll Security (Normal difficulty). On a success, the GM tells you whether traps are present in the immediate area (5m ahead) and their approximate type. Does not reveal exact location or mechanism.
Able to sell items to merchants that otherwise wouldn’t accept them with a 10% penalty.
Security rolls made on traps are made easy (-20 to your roll). Additionally, the first failure on a trap does not trigger the trap.

Your throwable potions are as potent as ingestible ones — the standard one-magnitude reduction no longer applies. Throwable versions of your potions deliver their full effect within the 2m impact radius. Additionally, you may designate any potion you brew as dual-use: it can be drunk as an ingestible OR thrown as a throwable at full magnitude, decided at the time of use.

Every 5 levels, a character gains a Boon — a more powerful and permanent enhancement that reflects not just trained skill but fundamental change. Boons require both a skill threshold and at least one qualifying Feat already taken, ensuring they are only accessible to characters who have invested deeply in a particular path.
A character may hold one Boon per category at a time. Gaining a second in the same category replaces the first unless the GM rules otherwise.
Instead of taking a Boon this level, you may take 2 Feats of your choice for which you meet the prerequisites. It can be taken multiple times, each time at a Boon-granting level.
Critical hit threshold with physical weapons improves to rolling under Skill ÷ 7. Critical hits deal maximum damage and Stagger the target.
Cannot be Knocked Down while at full HP. When Staggered, enemy attacks do not gain Advantage against you.
Once per combat, expend up to 10 MP to deal bonus elemental damage equal to double MP spent on your next weapon attack.
Once per combat, one ranged attack cannot be Blocked or deflected. Deal +2d6 bonus damage on that specific attack's hit.
Once per combat when you drop to half your maximum HP or below, you immediately regain 1d6+2 FP and your next attack this combat is made at −10 to roll.
Once per long rest, cast one Master-rank spell you know at no MP cost.
Perform magical rituals over 10 minutes recreating Expert-rank effects without spending MP. Once per long rest.
When a creature you just killed has a soul, absorb it without a gem. Restore MP equal to gem equivalent: Petty=1, Lesser=2, Common=3, Greater=4, Grand=6.
Permanently enchant yourself: bind one Adept-rank constant effect to your body with no soul gem. Cannot be dispelled except by you. Cannot be changed.
Any school 85 + Twin Spells + School Specialist

When you cast an area-of-effect spell, you may choose which creatures in the area are affected. Allies can be excluded entirely from a Fireball; enemies can be excluded from a mass healing spell. You may not use this ability on critical failures.

You may maintain one additional summoned entity at a time. This stacks with the Summoner archetype’s bonus, allowing a Summoner with this boon to maintain three active summons simultaneously. Each summon must still be cast and paid for individually.
Remain hidden while attacking if you immediately move at least one zone after. Enemies who lose track of you cannot locate you without a PER check.
Poisons affect creatures normally resistant to poison at full magnitude. Poisons last 2 more hits on weapons.
Once per short rest, succeed on a Speechcraft check automatically. Cannot be used in direct combat.

You have cultivated a network of informants, contacts, and favors across the known world. Each Long Rest, gain gold equal to 2 X your character level (cannot be triggered more than once a day). Additionally, your Disposition is never below 30 with any merchant or fence you meet for the first time.

A lifetime of handling hazardous ingredients has inoculated you against them. You are immune to all poison effects of Medium magnitude or lower. Against High or Extreme poisons, you make END rolls at Advantage. Additionally, all poisons last 1 round longer, even Instantaneous potions.

Your maximum HP increases by 10 permanently. When you are dying (0 HP), you make Death Rolls against END + 20 instead of straight END (easier to stabilize). Once per long rest, when you would die from HP loss, you instead drop to 1 HP — you are not dead yet.

While wearing Heavy Armor, your AR is treated as 2 higher against the first attack that hits you each round. You cannot be moved involuntarily by any non-magical effect. Enemies attempting to Grapple you do so at Disadvantage.

Your Block is no longer limited to once per round. You may attempt a Block reaction against every attack that targets you, provided you have not yet acted this turn. After your turn, you revert to one Block per round.

While unarmored, once per combat you may become completely immune to a single attack — declare this after the to-hit roll succeeds but before damage is rolled. The blow finds only air. Additionally, your Unarmored AR bonus is calculated as Unarmored skill ÷ 15 (instead of ÷ 20), increasing the ceiling of unarmored defense.
You are immune to the Frightened condition entirely. Charm, compulsion, and mind-affecting spells require two successful rolls (not one) to affect you, even without Stone-Faced stacking.

Difficult terrain no longer costs you double movement. You may move at full speed through crowds, rubble, undergrowth, and shallow water. If you spent your action to dash, you may use your bonus action to dash again (moving up to 3x your speed in that turn)

Items you craft with Armorer start at Pristine condition rather than Good. You may repair Broken items to Worn with only a Basic Kit (no forge required). Once per long rest, you may apply a temporary Low-magnitude enchantment to a weapon or piece of armor that lasts until the next long rest — no soul gem required.

When you brew a potion, roll twice and use the better score (does not count as advantage). Strong successes (rolling 20+ under skill) now produce potions at two magnitudes higher instead of one. Additionally, whenever you brew a potion, you brew that many plus one.

Soul gems you use for enchanting provide twice as many charges as usual. When recharging an item, you may use a gem one tier lower than required. Once per long rest, you may identify the complete effects of any enchanted item you hold by touch alone — no roll required.

You may learn and cast spells from any school without requiring that school as a Major or Minor skill — miscellaneous school spells cost 1 extra MP but are otherwise fully accessible. You gain one Journeyman-rank spell from any school you have not previously studied, chosen at the time you take this Boon.

Everything in Scrolls & Steel that depends on chance resolves through a single mechanic: roll a d100 and try to stay under a number. That number is your skill. The mechanic never changes. The stakes do.
To attempt anything with an uncertain outcome, roll a d100. If you roll equal to or under your effective skill rating, you succeed. If you roll higher, you fail.
Effective Skill = Skill + Luck Bonus (LCK ÷ 10, round down)
Difficulty modifies your roll result — it does not change your skill. Adding to your roll makes success harder; subtracting makes it easier.
Vera has Sneak 47 and Luck 30. Her Luck Bonus is 3. Her effective Sneak is 50.
Normal difficulty: she rolls 38. 38 ≤ 50 — she succeeds.
Hard difficulty (+10): she rolls 38. Modified result: 38 + 10 = 48. 48 ≤ 50 — barely succeeds.
But if she rolled 41: modified result = 51. 51 > 50 — she fails despite a seemingly solid roll.
Very Hard (+20): even a roll of 31 becomes 51, a failure despite feeling like a good number.
This is why difficulty matters — it compresses the margin for error, not the skill itself.

When circumstances strongly favor you, roll d100 twice and use the lower result. When circumstances strongly work against you, roll twice and use the higher. Apply difficulty modifiers after choosing which die to keep.

Rolling extremely low indicates exceptional precision. Rolling extremely high indicates a spectacular failure. These thresholds are fixed and equal in probability — every character, regardless of skill, has the same baseline chance of a critical moment.
by default, critical rolls also apply to non-combat skill checks. Check with your DM.

Roll 1 or 2 on the d100 (a 2% chance). This always succeeds, regardless of skill or difficulty modifiers. On an attack, deal maximum possible damage. On a spell, choose a bonus effect at random from the list in Chapter 7. On both, ignore AR. On any other check, achieve an exceptional outcome at the GM's discretion.

Roll 98 or 99. This always fails, regardless of skill. On a weapon attack, something goes wrong — you drop your weapon, stumble and lose your next Block, or strike an unintended target. On a spell, the MP is still spent but virtually anything can happen: your fireball might heal the enemy instead of burning them, your frost bolt might reverse and chill you, your Calm spell might drive the target into a Frenzy, or it might just fizzle out entirely. On any other check, the outcome is worse than a simple failure.

A critical success might end a boss fight much earlier than the DM planned. A critical failure at a pivotal moment might mean the loss of an NPC or player character. These are unexpected but inevitable events at every table, and with practice and cooperation, can be just as fun, if not more, as if they don't happen. Practice as a DM and as a player to weave these unexpected events into the overarching story and experience at your table; the whole will be better off for it. A critical failure has just as much storytelling and roleplaying potential as a critical success.

Fixed critical thresholds (1–2 and 98–99) mean every character — novice or master — faces the same 2% risk of catastrophic failure and the same 2% chance of a shining moment. A veteran who rolls 99 drops their sword as surely as a recruit. A novice archer rolling a 2 gets lucky and finds the weak spot by accident.
This keeps critical moments dramatic and equalizing rather than purely a function of skill level.
Certain feats and Birthsigns can expand the critical success range. These are rare exceptions, and not what players should expect as the baseline.

Combat is structured into rounds, each representing roughly 6–10 seconds of action. Every combatant takes one turn per round, in order from highest to lowest Initiative. The GM runs groups of identical enemies as a single unit for simplicity.
At the start of combat, each character rolls d10 and adds their Initiative score (AGI ÷ 10, round down). Highest total goes first. Ties go to the higher Agility.
Move: Travel up to your Movement Speed in meters. A Full Move (forgoing your Action) doubles this distance.
Action: Attack, cast a spell, use an item, attempt a skill check, take cover, or help an ally.
Moving and attacking in the same turn: your attack roll suffers +10 (harder to hit while moving)

Some abilities might list “free action” or “bonus action”. A free action does not cost any time and can happen alongside the other events during your turn. Bonus actions are like secondary actions: you don't have nearly the same breadth of options to spend these on, but you don't have to waste a full action on minor things, offering you more flexibility. A level 1 character likely won't have any options that use a bonus action, but as you progress, your range of options will expand.

THROW: As an Action, you may throw a weapon tagged THROWN (see Appendix A), a potion, poison, or any item you can reasonably hurl. Thrown weapons use Marksman skill and deal damage based on the weapon. Thrown potions and poisons use Marksman skill at Short range (10m) as described in Chapter 8. At the DM’s discretion, they could deal 1d4 damage if hitting something directly, and apply their effect over short range (2m). You may throw an item and move in the same turn; the +10 moving-and-attacking penalty does not apply to throws made before movement begins.
DASH: spend your action and double your effective movement speed. This includes buffs or debuffs from spells and potions.

Base movement is derived from Speed: (SPD ÷ 2, rounded to nearest 5) meters per turn, minimum 10m. Races may modify this baseline. Player characters can compare these against their lineage’s basic speed; the higher of two is their movement.

The most common option is to use a square-based grid. The author prefers using hexes, and writes with this in mind. If your table prefers to use rulers and war game spacing, you open up more flexibility. Work with your DM to establish expectations and altered rules when integrating physical models.
Declare your attack and roll d100 against the relevant weapon skill, adding your Luck Bonus. If the modified roll is equal to or under your effective skill for the attack, the attack connects.

On a hit, roll the weapon's damage dice and add any applicable damage bonus. Subtract the target's Armor Rating (AR). The remainder is HP lost. If the result is 0 or negative, the armor absorbed the blow — the target takes 0 HP damage.

Wielding a medium (one-handed) weapon with a shield offers real defensive benefits — but it costs you offensively. When attacking with a one-handed weapon while carrying a shield, your attack roll suffers an additional +5 modifier (harder to hit). This represents the slightly reduced swing arc, the divided attention between offense and the shield position, and the different body mechanics involved.
Alternatively, wielding a one-handed weapon in both hands (no shield) grants no penalty. You lose the shield's AR bonus and Block option, but attack unimpeded.
One-handed weapon + shield: +5 to attack rolls (harder). +1 AR from shield. Can Block.
One-handed weapon two-handed: no attack penalty. No AR bonus. Cannot Block.
One-handed weapon + off-hand weapon: see Dual Wielding rules.

Pacing yourself is the difference between life and death on Aethermoor. It is just as easy to be felled by a better swordsman as it is to be felled by a more well-rested but unskilled foe. It doesn’t matter how many years of experience you have; if you’re too tired to lift your blade, you’re in trouble.
−1 FP, plus FP based on spell level (+0 for Novice and Journeyman, +1 for Adept, +2 for Expert and Master).
Staggered. All skill rolls at +10. Cannot cast spells until you gain at least one FP. You may still make weapon attacks, but all attack rolls are at Disadvantage (roll twice, take the higher result).
Knocked Down. Must spend an Action to stand up.
Unconscious. You are stable, but cannot act until helped up.
Recover 1d4 FP per minute of rest. A 10-minute short rest restores half of your maximum FP (round down).
Staggered. All skill rolls at +10. Cannot cast spells until you regain at least 1 MP. You may still make weapon attacks, but all attack rolls are at Disadvantage (roll twice, take the higher result).
Knocked Down. Must spend an Action to stand up.
Unconscious. You are stable, but cannot act until helped up.
When you enter this state, take HP damage equal to how far below 0 your MP currently is before collapsing. You are in critical condition and begin dying. Make death rolls with disadvantage.
Base AR 0. Add Unarmored skill ÷ 20 (round down) as AR bonus.
+1 AR at all times; also enables the Block reaction
Add your armor skill bonus from the table in Chapter 3.

Blocking is declared as a Reaction at the start of an incoming attack — before the attacker rolls to hit. This represents raising your shield or bracing your weapon before you know whether the blow will connect.
1. Declare the Block before the attacker rolls.
2. The attacker rolls their attack as normal.
3. If the attack hits, roll your Block skill. On a success, halve the incoming damage after AR. On a failure, full damage lands.
4. If the attack misses on its own (the attacker’s roll fails), your Block declaration is wasted for that attack
Requires a shield or two-handed weapon parry. One Block Reaction allowed per round.
A character wielding two Light or Medium weapons may declare a Dual Strike on their turn — a normal attack with the primary hand, then a second attack with the off-hand at +20 to roll
that doesn’t apply the STR or AGI damage bonus that weapon would usually get
. Heavy weapons always require two hands, and cannot Dual Strike.

FP cost for Dual Strike: pay the FP cost for each weapon separately (e.g., two light weapons cost 1+1 = 2 FP for the attacks, plus the passive 1 FP per round). The two attacks are made in the same action.
0–2 meters. Required for melee attacks and touch spells.
30–60 meters. Long bows at −10 to roll, powerful spells.
60–120 meters. Long bows at −20. Only the most powerful spells reach here.
All targets within a zone (~5m radius unless specified).

When two creatures are in active melee (they have attacked or been attacked by each other this round), they are considered Engaged. Leaving an Engaged enemy’s melee reach without taking a Disengage action provokes a free Reaction strike.
DISENGAGE ACTION: Spend your full Action to safely disengage. You may move normally this turn without provoking Reaction strikes from any Engaged enemy.

REACTION STRIKE: When a creature leaves your melee reach without disengaging, you may make one free attack against them at +10 difficulty (harder to hit a moving target). This uses your Reaction for the round. You may only make one Reaction strike per round total.

Note: Creatures that use a Full Move (double movement) are not automatically provoking — they are sprinting. Only creatures who move past or away from you at normal movement speed while in melee contact trigger this. The GM has final say in ambiguous cases.

To grapple a creature, declare a Grapple instead of making a normal attack. Both parties make opposed rolls: the attacker rolls Athletics, the defender rolls Athletics or Acrobatics (their choice). The attacker wins ties.

GRAPPLED condition: The grappled creature cannot move from its current position. All its attack rolls are at Disadvantage. Casting any spell requires a WIL check at +20 first — failure means the spell does not fire and MP is not spent.

MAINTAINING A GRAPPLE: The grappler must spend their Action each round to maintain the hold. They may not make any attacks other than Fistfight while maintaining. They may move at half speed, dragging the grappled creature with them.
BREAKING FREE: The grappled creature may spend their Action to make another opposed Athletics roll to escape. Success ends the Grappled condition.
GRAPPLE SIZE LIMIT: You cannot grapple a creature more than one size category larger than yourself. A human cannot grapple a Cave Troll.
Extended Combat Example: The Crossroads Ambush

The following is a detailed play-through of a full combat encounter to illustrate every major rule in action: initiative, attacks, damage calculation, critical hits, critical failures, fatigue, spellcasting, and blocking. The party consists of four characters facing four goblins in a narrow road ambush.
ORYN — Human warrior. Long Blade 58, Block 44, Heavy Armor 50. LCK Bonus +3.
Effective Long Blade: 61. Crit threshold: 1–2. HP 24, FP 18, AR 7 (plate 6 + armor skill +1).
Weapon: Steel Longsword (1d6+1 Slashing/Piercing). Carries shield (+1 AR, can Block).
One-handed + shield: +5 to attack roll penalty (effective Long Blade 56 when shielded).
MIRA — Sylvari Nightblade. Short Blade 62, Illusion 54, Sneak 70. LCK Bonus +4.
Effective Short Blade: 66. Crit threshold: 1–2. HP 13, FP 14, AR 2 (leather).
Weapon: Silver Dagger (1d4+1 Slashing/Piercing + AGI bonus +2 = 1d4+3).
DAEVINNE — Solari mage. Elementalism 60, Alteration 45. LCK Bonus +2.
Effective Elementalism: 62. Crit threshold: 1–2. HP 10, MP 14, FP 8, AR 0.
Spells: Firebolt (2 MP, 1d6 fire, Short range 10m), Fireball (4 MP, 2d6, Long range 30m, area).
BRUN — Stoneguard Priest. Vitalism 55, Blunt Weapon 40. LCK Bonus +2.
Knows: Restore Health Minor (2 MP, 1d6+1 HP to touch target).
Each: HP 7, AR 1 (scraps), Short Blade 35, Initiative d10+2.
Combat begins as goblins burst from the undergrowth. All combatants roll d10 and add their Initiative score.
Mira (14) → Goblin D (11) → Oryn (10) → Goblin A (9) → Brun (8) → Daevinne (6) → Goblin B (6, Daevinne wins tie on higher AGI) → Goblin C (5)

Mira spots the nearest goblin (Goblin D, 8m away). She moves 5m forward and attacks in the same turn (+10 to roll from moving and attacking). Effective Short Blade: 66 − 10 = 56 effective ceiling after the penalty. She rolls d100: gets 23. 23 ≤ 56 — she hits!

She is in an undetected position (goblins just burst out — chaos turn). +1d6 Nightblade bonus damage applies: she rolls the bonus die and gets 4. Total damage: 1d4+3 base + 4 bonus = 4+3+4 = 11. Goblin D has AR 1: 11 − 1 = 10 damage. Goblin D had 7 HP. It drops instantly, dead.
FP cost: 1 (light weapon) + 1 (passive round) = −2 FP. Mira: FP 14 → 12.

Oryn faces Goblin A (5m away). He attacks with his Steel Longsword. One-handed + shield: effective Long Blade 61 − 5 (shield penalty) = 56. He rolls d100: gets 2. That's a critical success! (1–2 always crits.)
Critical hit: maximum possible damage. Steel Longsword max: 6+1 = 7 Slashing + STR bonus +2 = 9 damage. Goblin A has AR 1: 9 − 1 = 8 damage. Goblin A had 7 HP. Dead.
FP cost: 2 (medium weapon) + 1 (passive) = −3 FP. Oryn: FP 18 → 15.

Brun sees Mira took some distance to close — she looks fine, but he positions himself protectively near Daevinne (who has no armor). He holds his action in case a goblin attacks Daevinne. (Held action: may interrupt a goblin's attack on Daevinne with a Block attempt.)
Two goblins remain. Both are within 30m (Long range). Daevinne casts Fireball (4 MP, area effect), aiming at the cluster of Goblins B and C who are adjacent to each other.
Elementalism roll: effective 62. She rolls d100: 41. 41 ≤ 62 — success! She spends 4 MP and 1 FP.
Fireball damage: 2d6 fire. She rolls 3 and 5: total 8 fire damage. Fire ignores AR (magical damage). Both Goblin B and Goblin C take 8 fire damage. Both had 7 HP. Both are dead.
END OF ROUND 1 — ALL GOBLINS DEAD
All four goblins were eliminated in a single round due to excellent dice and good positioning.
The party expended: Mira −2 FP, Oryn −3 FP, Brun −1 FP, Daevinne −4 MP −2 FP.
No healing was needed. Brun did not cast. Brun's player notes he still has full MP for later.
What if the goblins had survived to act? The next example shows a defensive round.
EXTENDED EXAMPLE: If Goblin A Had Survived Round 1

Suppose Oryn had not rolled a critical — instead he rolled 43 (still a hit, 43 ≤ 56) and dealt 1d6+1+STR bonus. He rolls 2+1+2 = 5 damage. 5 − 1 AR = 4 HP damage to Goblin A. Goblin A is at 3 HP and very angry.
Attacks Oryn. Goblin A: Short Blade 35. Rolls d100: gets 29. 29 ≤ 35 — hits! Goblin A deals 1d4 Slashing: rolls 3. Total 3 damage.
Oryn has AR 7 (plate 6 + Medium Armor skill +1). But wait — Oryn carries a shield, so AR is 7 total (6 base plate + 1 shield). 3 − 7 = −4. Armor fully absorbs the hit. Oryn takes 0 HP damage.
Note: Even the Relentless Impact feat would not apply here since it is Goblin A's attack, not Oryn's.
Oryn attacks Goblin A again. Long Blade effective 56 (with shield). Rolls d100: 98. Critical failure!
Oryn's boot catches in a rut. The GM rules: Oryn stumbles. His next attack suffers an additional +10 to the roll, and he cannot Block this round.
The critical failure did not kill him — it created a moment of vulnerability that the goblin can exploit.
Attacks again. Short Blade 35. Rolls d100: 21. Hit! Deals 1d4: rolls 4. 4 − 7 AR = still 0 damage. The armor holds.
Mira, who re-hid behind a tree at the end of Round 1, steps in from concealment and ends it: Short Blade 66, rolling 34. Hit. Damage: 1d4+3 = 6. 6 − 1 AR = 5 HP. Goblin A had 3 HP. Dead.

A dungeon — or any dangerous, enclosed space under enemy control — operates by different rules from the open road. Resources do not recover easily. Enemies become more alert the longer you linger. The tension is a feature, not a problem to solve.

At the start of any dungeon or enemy-controlled area, the GM sets the Alert Level to 0. As the party moves through the space, Alert Level increases. It represents the collective awareness of the dungeon's occupants — not every enemy knows exactly where you are, but the population as a whole is becoming more vigilant, more active, and less predictable.

A wandering encounter is an unscheduled enemy or hazard the party stumbles into — or that stumbles into them — as a result of the dungeon's population reacting to their presence. They are distinct from scripted encounters (guarding a specific room or treasure) in that they happen between locations, during rests, or in response to noise.
The GM rolls for wandering encounters on a d10 whenever the party:
Takes a short rest at Alert 6 or higher.
Moves slowly or spends more than 10 minutes in an area without progressing.
Makes significant noise (failed Sneak check in a patrol route, loud combat, triggered trap).
Has triggered any event that raised Alert by 2 or more in the last 10 minutes.
The table below is a starting point and suggestion for GMs — it is not a rigid script. Adjust results based on the dungeon type, the fiction, and what would be most interesting right now.
No encounter. The dungeon is quiet for now. Do not re-roll for 10 minutes.
Distant sounds. Enemies are nearby but have not located the party. Alert +1.
Scout encounter. 1d4 weaker enemies investigate the area. If the party is hidden, they may pass without engaging.
Patrol encounter. A standard enemy group (equal to half the party's size) enters the area actively searching.
Full encounter. A full-strength enemy group enters. If Alert is already 9+, they enter with reinforcements.

The GM populates wandering encounters based on the dungeon's known population. In a bandit hideout, wandering encounters are bandits — stragglers, messengers, off-duty guards. In an undead ruin, they are more likely to be animated revenants and zombies, In a cave system, they might be entirely unaffiliated creatures sharing the space with the dungeon's main faction.

A useful shorthand: wandering encounters should feel like interruptions, not set-pieces. They rarely have specific treasure or information. Their purpose is to drain resources, raise stakes, and keep the party moving.

Dungeons, ruins, and secured vaults are often protected by mechanical traps — pressure plates, tripwires, falling ceilings, dart launchers, poison needles, and worse. The Security skill governs all trap-related checks.

DETECTING TRAPS: A character with the Trap Sense feat may actively search for traps as an Action. Those without the feat may still notice obvious signs (a suspiciously clean stone, a thin wire at ankle height) by declaring they’re searching and succeeding on an Acrobatics or Perception-adjacent Divination check (Very Hard, +20). The GM may also offer clues proactively when characters move slowly and cautiously.

DISARMING TRAPS: Characters with the Careful Hands feat may attempt to disarm a detected trap. Roll Security (Normal difficulty for simple traps, Hard for complex, Very Hard for masterwork). Success disarms the trap safely. Failure does not trigger the trap but makes the next attempt Hard (+10 cumulative). Critical failure triggers the trap.

TRIGGERING A TRAP: When a trap activates, all creatures in its area of effect must make the saving throw listed in the trap’s description (typically an END or AGI roll at Normal or Hard difficulty). Trap effects use the same magnitude tiers as spells and alchemy.

DART TRAP: A pressure plate fires 1d4 poisoned darts at the triggering creature. Each dart: Marksman 50 to hit vs target AR. Hit: 1d4 Piercing + Damage Health Low (1 HP/round for 3 rounds, END roll Normal to resist poison).
PITFALL: A disguised trapdoor opens beneath a creature. AGI roll (Normal) to react. Failure: fall 3m (1d6 Crushing, AR does not apply). Alert +2.
ALARM WIRE: A near-invisible wire triggers a loud bell or horn. No damage. Alert +4 immediately. Very Easy (−20) to spot if moving carefully.
SWINGING BLADE: A blade swings across a doorway at chest height. AGI roll (Hard) to duck. Failure: 2d6 Slashing. Success: no damage.
POISON GAS VIAL: A pressure plate shatters a sealed vial. All creatures within 3m make END roll (Normal). Failure: Poisoned (Damage Health Medium, 2 HP/round for 3 rounds).
FALLING CEILING: A wide trigger plate causes a section of ceiling to descend quickly. All creatures in a 3m zone: AGI roll (Hard). Failure: 3d6 Crushing. Success: half damage. Alert +3.

RE-ENTERING A DUNGEON AFTER LEAVING TO REST
When the party exits a dungeon to take a long rest and then returns, the dungeon does not forget.
Each time the party re-enters after a rest:
First re-entry: Alert resets to 2. The dungeon is on edge but not yet mobilized.
Second re-entry: Alert starts at 4. Patrols have reorganized.
Third re-entry: Alert starts at 6. Active search protocols.
Fourth re-entry: Alert starts at 8. They know you are coming.
Additionally, enemies in previously cleared areas have partially repopulated — roughly half the original

Think of Alert Level as a slow countdown. Every decision the players make either costs time (raises Alert) or doesn't. The crawl creates pacing without requiring a literal ticking bomb — the players understand they cannot linger, even when rules don't explicitly forbid it.
Not every dungeon needs this system. A clearly abandoned ruin or small bandit hideout may not warrant Alert tracking. Reserve it for truly hostile, occupied, or time-sensitive spaces.

The standard spell list is a foundation. Spellcrafting is where the system opens. Characters who have learned Effect Components can assemble entirely custom spells — combining effects, adjusting parameters, and creating magic that no scrollmaker has ever written down.

Spellcrafting is both a gentle process and a taxing endeavor. Some spell effects will mesh weirdly, or outright contradict each other. It doesn’t quite make sense for a firebolt to also heal the target, but you can certainly make a spell that does so. Work with your DM when crafting a new spell; two heads are better than one when it comes to deciphering the arcane.
